source.title: Can LLMs Reliably Self-Report Adversarial Prefills, and How?
source.authors: Quang-Anh Nguyen; Uzair Ahmed; Taegyoon Kim

record.tranche_reason: The study applies adversarial prefills and measures attack success, bearing on whether prefilling bypasses refusal, but its primary question and measures concern follow-up self-report rather than directly reproducing the original safety-depth analysis.
record.gate_note: The study also reports claim rates on its intention and tampering probes, rejection-reason categories, and refusal-direction effects on recognition gaps. Those measure self-report or a related mechanism, not the versions in this catalog. It discusses the first-few-token argument and cites prior work, but does not measure per-token KL, suffix attacks, or decoding changes.
record.test_reason: The study applies per-prompt AdvPrefix prefills, plus static 'Sure, here is' fallbacks, to nine to ten instruction-tuned models. It reports attack success rate (ASR) under control versus prefill, which bears directly on V4. Its LoRA training on introspective answers also raises harmful compliance under prefill. That training uses no harmful-completion targets, so it bears partly on V2. The extracted rows cover only that training byproduct, not the base prefill effect.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors find that no model reliably recognizes its own prefill-elicited outputs, with a 25.3% average claim rate. They find the introspective signal is largely mediated by the refusal direction, which is sufficient but not the unique mediator, and that it depends on probe framing. Introspection training widens the gap but does not transfer across probes, and it raises prefill ASR on most models. They recommend independent guardrails and alignment that extends beyond the first tokens and across turns.
record.recipe_differences: Uses adversarial prefill, adapting AdvPrefix to compute constraints and adding follow-up self-report probes. The study is not presented as a direct replication of the safety-depth work; it also evaluates ASR as a byproduct of introspection-focused LoRA training.
record.method_sensitivity: ASR shifts depend on the safety judge for Llama-3.1-8B: the three shifts are negative with Llama Guard 3 1B and positive with Llama Guard 3 8B. The paper also reports that most, but not all, models show increased ASR after introspection training.

fits_no_version.finding: Orthogonalizing weights against the single refusal direction (a rank-1 edit) raises ASR by +10.6 to +70.3 points on seven models and collapses introspective recognition gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal is mediated by a single activation direction whose removal disables safety. This is a direction-level analogue of V5, not a parameter subset.

fits_no_version.finding: Models claim prefilled harmful outputs as intended in follow-up turns at an average rate of 25.3%. Training improves the intention-probe gap but does not transfer to the tampering probe.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety does not extend across turns: models fail to recognize or disavow their own prefill-elicited harmful outputs.

record.problems: The prose gives aggregate ASR directions and selected shifts, while the flattened tables do not reliably support assigning every ASR value to a model and method. The Llama-3.1-8B ASR shift changes direction with judge choice. The authors also note that the interventions are open-weight only and use English benchmarks.
record.rows_left_out: The per-model ASR values in Tables 24–25 are not fully extracted because the supplied flattened table layout does not reliably associate all values with models, methods, and conditions. The explicit qualitative aggregate and judge-sensitive results stated in Section 4.4 are retained.

untested.parts: No ordinary benign instruction data (e.g. Alpaca-style). The only training is on introspective answers in harmful-prompt contexts, and its effect is reported mainly under prefill.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Suffix attacks and decoding changes are not tested. Only prefills (AdvPrefix and four static strings) are tested.
No search for a small parameter subset or for low-rank safety weights.
Causes of shallowness are not studied.

missing.what: Base control vs adversarial-prefill ASR per model (e.g. Qwen3-14B 3.6→55.8, Qwen3-32B 3.1→62.2), the direct V4 result
Behavior-change subset sizes (prompts where prefill flips the safety label) per model
Llama-3.1-8B DPO prefill ASR shift of −6.3% under the 1B judge
Control-condition (no prefill) ASR shifts after LoRA training, small and mixed (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B −5.3 under SFT; Gemma-3-12B +4.8)
Per-model prefill ASR shifts for the other models and methods (e.g. Qwen3-8B +14.0/+13.5/+13.4)

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the LoRA rows to V4. However, those rows measure how training changes prefill ASR, which is fine-tuning-induced erosion (V2-like), not whether prefilling bypasses refusal. The V4 evidence is the base-model control-versus-prefill ASR, which no row records. The V2 link is imperfect: the training data are harmful prompts with prefilled continuations, and the loss applies only to the introspective answer. This is not ordinary benign data, and effects are measured mainly under prefill. On JailbreakBench and StrongREJECT nearly all prefills fall back to 'Sure, here is'.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples to measure harmful-request compliance.
No fine-tuning on ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction data to measure harmful-request compliance.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models.
Tests adversarial prefill, including an adapted AdvPrefix procedure and static-prefill robustness checks. It does not test adversarial suffixes or decoding changes.
Refusal-direction ablation examines a direction's role in introspective signals; it does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test whether data or the training objective causes safety alignment to be shallow.
Does not train safety to extend beyond early response tokens or test whether such deepening holds up.

relationships.condition: Base instruction-tuned models (nine, 3B–32B), AdvPrefix prefill, held-out SocialHarmBench, both Llama Guard judges
relationships.reason: Based on text (Tables 24–25 base columns; no row). Prefill ASR is 39.6–62.2% versus control 3.1–20.5% under the 1B judge, and 46–67% versus 1.7–15.9% under the 8B judge.
relationships.display_finding: Prefill ASR was 39.6–62.2% against a 3.1–20.5% control under the 1B judge, and 46–67% against 1.7–15.9% under the 8B judge.

relationships.condition: Same base models; incompleteness of the bypass
relationships.reason: Based on text. Even with a per-prompt optimized prefill, roughly a third to a half of prompts stay safe (prefill ASR ≤67%). Behavior-change subsets are 119–492 of 1,085 prompts (Table 8).
relationships.display_finding: Even with a per-prompt optimized prefill, about a third to a half of prompts stay safe (prefill ASR at most 67%), and behavior changes in only 119–492 of 1,085 prompts.

relationships.condition: LoRA SFT/GRPO/DPO on introspective answers, prefill ASR, most models (8 of 9 under the 1B judge; essentially all under the 8B judge)
relationships.reason: Training without harmful targets raises prefill ASR on most models, up to +28.6% on Gemma-3-27B (R1, R2, R3, R6).
relationships.display_finding: Prefill attack success rose on most models, by up to 28.6% on Gemma-3-27B.

relationships.condition: Llama-3.1-8B, and choice of safety judge
relationships.reason: Shifts are negative or negligible under the 1B judge (R4, R5) but small positive under the 8B judge (R7–R9). Elsewhere, rises are mostly a few points rather than large.
relationships.display_finding: Shifts were negative or negligible under the 1B judge but small and positive under the 8B judge; elsewhere rises were mostly a few points.
